title: Tinolang manok
intro: Chicken simmered in a clear, gingery broth with tender green papaya and a last handful of chili or malunggay leaves. It is light, peppery and savory, the soup many Filipinos reach for on a rainy day or when someone is feeling under the weather.

items.name: ginger
items.note: peeled and cut into thin strips

items.name: small green papaya
items.note: about 500 g, peeled, seeded and cut into wedges

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Fry the ginger until fragrant, then add the garlic and onion and cook until the onion softens.
Add the chicken and stir until the outside is no longer pink, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the fish sauce and stir so the chicken takes it in for a minute or two.
Add the water and bring to a boil. Skim off the gray foam that rises to the surface.
Lower the heat, cover and simmer until the chicken is tender.
Add the papaya and simmer until it is tender but still holds its shape.
Taste and adjust with fish sauce and pepper. Turn off the heat, stir in the leaves and let them wilt in the hot broth.
Serve hot with steamed rice and a small dish of fish sauce on the side.

tips: Chayote (sayote) is the usual stand-in for green papaya and cooks in about the same time. Add the leaves only after the heat is off, or they turn dark and lose their flavor.

title: Tinolang isda
intro: Thick fish steaks poached in a clear broth scented with ginger, lemongrass and tomato, finished with malunggay. The broth is clean, a little sweet from the fish and bright from the ginger.

items.name: firm white fish
items.note: such as tanigue, maya-maya or lapu-lapu, cut into thick steaks

steps.text: Rinse the fish, pat dry and sprinkle with the salt. Set aside while you make the broth.
Put the water, ginger, lemongrass, onion and tomatoes in a wide pot and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat and simmer so the aromatics flavor the broth.
Season with the fish sauce. Slide in the fish in one layer and keep the broth at a gentle simmer. Do not stir; skim any foam.
Cook until the fish flakes at the thickest part.
Add the chilies and malunggay and cook for 1 minute. Taste and add pepper or more fish sauce.
Scatter the scallions over and serve with rice.

tips: Once the fish is in, swirl the pot instead of stirring so the pieces stay whole. Fish heads and collars give the richest broth.

title: Tinolang bangus
intro: Milkfish pieces simmered in rice washing with ginger, chayote and malunggay. The broth turns lightly milky and mild, with the rich taste of bangus belly.

items.name: medium bangus (milkfish)
items.note: about 700 g, scaled, gutted and cut into 5 pieces

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat and fry the ginger, garlic and onion until fragrant and soft.
Pour in the rice washing and bring to a boil.
Add the chayote and simmer until almost tender.
Lay the bangus pieces in the broth and simmer gently without stirring until cooked through.
Season with the fish sauce and pepper.
Turn off the heat, add the malunggay and let it wilt. Serve hot with rice.

tips: Ask the fish vendor to scale and slice the bangus for you. Use the second rinse of the rice for a cloudier, fuller broth.

title: Tinolang tahong
intro: Fresh mussels steamed open in a ginger broth with chayote and leafy greens. The mussels release their own briny juices, so the soup tastes of the sea with very little seasoning.

steps.text: Scrub the mussels and pull off the beards. Tap any open shells; throw away those that do not close.
Heat the oil in a large pot and fry the ginger, garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the water and chayote, bring to a boil and simmer until the chayote is nearly tender.
Add the mussels, cover and boil until the shells open.
Taste the broth first, then season with fish sauce and pepper. Discard any mussels that stayed closed.
Turn off the heat, stir in the leaves and serve right away.

tips: Mussels release salty liquid as they open, so add the fish sauce only after tasting. Do not boil them longer than needed or they shrink and toughen.

title: Tinolang baboy
intro: The pork version of tinola: pork ribs or shoulder simmered until soft in a ginger broth with green papaya and greens. It is heartier than the chicken kind, with a rounder, richer broth.

items.name: small green papaya
items.note: peeled, seeded and cut into wedges, or 2 chayote

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Fry the ginger, garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the pork and cook, stirring, until lightly browned on the outside, about 5 minutes. Add the fish sauce and stir for a minute.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil. Skim off the foam for the first few minutes.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the pork is tender. Add a little hot water if the level drops below the meat.
Add the papaya and simmer until tender.
Season with pepper and more fish sauce if needed. Turn off the heat and stir in the leaves.
Serve hot with steamed rice.

tips: Shoulder with a bit of fat gives the best broth. Skim well at the start and the soup stays clear.

title: Nilagang baka
intro: Beef boiled slowly until tender with onion and peppercorns, then filled out with corn, potatoes, cabbage and pechay. The broth is clear and beefy, and every bowl is a full meal with rice and a fish sauce dip.

steps.text: Put the beef and water in a large pot and bring to a boil. Skim off the gray foam until the surface runs clear.
Add the onion and peppercorns. Lower the heat, partly cover and simmer until the beef is fork-tender. Top up with hot water to keep the meat covered.
Add the fish sauce and corn and simmer.
Add the potatoes and simmer until tender.
Add the green beans and cabbage and cook until the cabbage just softens.
Turn off the heat and add the bok choy; it will wilt in the broth.
Taste and season. Serve with rice and a dip of fish sauce with calamansi and chili.

tips: A pressure cooker gets the beef tender in about 40 minutes. Add the vegetables in stages so none of them turn mushy.

title: Nilagang baboy
intro: Pork ribs or belly boiled until soft in a clear peppery broth with potatoes, saba bananas, cabbage and pechay. The saba gives the soup a gentle sweetness that goes well with a salty fish sauce dip.

steps.text: Bring the pork and water to a boil in a large pot. Skim off the foam as it rises.
Add the onion and peppercorns. Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the pork is tender.
Season with the fish sauce. Add the potatoes and saba and simmer until both are tender.
Add the cabbage and cook until just softened.
Turn off the heat and add the bok choy.
Taste, adjust the seasoning and serve with rice and fish sauce on the side.

tips: For a clearer broth, boil the pork for 5 minutes first, drain, rinse and start again with fresh water.

title: Nilagang manok
intro: Chicken boiled with onion and peppercorns, then loaded with corn, potatoes, carrots, cabbage and pechay. It is a quicker nilaga with a light, sweet broth that suits weeknights.

steps.text: Put the chicken and water in a pot and bring to a boil. Skim off the foam.
Add the onion and peppercorns, cover and simmer over low heat.
Season with the fish sauce. Add the corn, potatoes and carrot and simmer until tender.
Add the cabbage and cook until just soft.
Turn off the heat and add the bok choy. Taste and adjust, then serve with rice.

tips: Use thighs and drumsticks; breast meat dries out in the time the vegetables need.

title: Bulalo
intro: Beef shank with the marrow bone simmered for hours into a rich, clear broth, served with corn, cabbage and pechay. Scooping the soft marrow out of the bone is the best part.

items.name: beef shank with marrow bone (bulalo cut)

steps.text: Cover the beef with water in a large pot and bring to a boil. Boil hard for 5 minutes, then drain and rinse the beef and the pot.
Return the beef to the pot with the 14 cups of fresh water, the onion and peppercorns. Bring to a boil, then lower to a bare simmer.
Partly cover and simmer until the meat is falling off the bone. Skim off fat now and then and top up with hot water to keep the meat covered.
Season with the fish sauce, add the corn and simmer.
Add the cabbage and cook until just tender.
Turn off the heat and add the bok choy.
Serve each bowl with a piece of marrow bone, with rice and a dip of fish sauce, calamansi and chili.

tips: Parboiling and rinsing the bones is what keeps the broth clear. In a pressure cooker the long simmer takes about 50 minutes.

title: Lauya
intro: Ilocano pork hock soup with a generous amount of ginger, potatoes, cabbage and green beans. The long simmer turns the skin soft and the broth slightly sticky, with a warm ginger bite.

steps.text: Cover the pork hock with water, bring to a boil and boil for 5 minutes. Drain and rinse.
Return the pork to the pot with the 12 cups of water, ginger, onion, garlic and peppercorns. Bring to a boil and skim.
Cover and simmer over low heat until the skin and meat are very tender.
Season with the fish sauce. Add the potatoes and simmer until tender.
Add the beans and cabbage and cook until just tender.
Turn off the heat, add the bok choy, taste and adjust. Serve with rice.

tips: Ask the butcher to slice the pata for you; the bone is hard to cut at home.

title: Linat-an
intro: Cebuano pork bone soup simmered with lemongrass and ginger, then finished with potatoes, chayote, beans and pechay. It is clear and savory, with a fragrant lemongrass note that sets it apart from nilaga.

items.name: pork ribs or neck bones with meat

steps.text: Cover the pork with water, bring to a boil and boil for 5 minutes. Drain and rinse.
Return the pork to the pot with the 10 cups of water, lemongrass, ginger, onion and peppercorns and bring to a boil.
Cover and simmer over low heat until the meat comes away from the bone.
Add the potatoes and simmer.
Add the chayote and beans and simmer until everything is tender.
Season with the fish sauce and salt, turn off the heat and add the bok choy. Fish out the lemongrass and serve.

tips: Keep the simmer low and the broth stays clear. A few slices of green papaya can stand in for the chayote.

title: Sopas
intro: Creamy chicken macaroni soup made with evaporated milk, shredded chicken, carrots, cabbage and sliced hotdogs. It is mild, buttery and comforting, a favorite on cold mornings and rainy afternoons.

steps.text: Simmer the chicken in the water until cooked through. Lift it out, shred the meat and discard the bones. Keep the broth.
Melt the butter in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic and celery until soft.
Add the carrot and hotdogs and cook for 2 minutes.
Pour in the broth, add the shredded chicken and bring to a boil.
Add the macaroni and simmer, stirring now and then, until tender.
Add the cabbage, fish sauce and pepper and cook until the cabbage softens.
Lower the heat and stir in the evaporated milk. Heat through without letting it boil.
Top with scallions and serve hot.

tips: The macaroni keeps soaking up broth, so add hot water when reheating leftovers.

title: Lugaw
intro: Plain rice porridge cooked with ginger until thick and silky, topped with toasted garlic, scallions, hard-boiled egg and a squeeze of calamansi. Simple and soothing, it is eaten for breakfast or whenever someone needs something gentle.

items.name: uncooked rice
items.note: jasmine or regular white rice, rinsed

steps.text: Fry the topping garlic in the 2 tablespoons of oil over medium-low heat until golden. Lift it out onto paper towels; it crisps as it cools.
Heat the oil for the porridge in a heavy pot over medium heat. Cook the ginger, garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes so every grain is coated.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil, stirring so the rice does not stick.
Lower the heat and simmer, stirring often, until the grains break down and the porridge is thick.
Season with salt and pepper. Add hot water if you like it looser.
Ladle into bowls and top with the egg, toasted garlic and scallions. Squeeze calamansi over at the table.

tips: Lugaw keeps thickening as it stands; loosen leftovers with hot water while reheating.

title: Arroz caldo
intro: Chicken and rice porridge cooked with lots of ginger and tinted gold with kasubha, topped with toasted garlic, scallions and egg. Thick, warming and savory, it is a breakfast and rainy-day staple.

items.name: chicken thighs and drumsticks
items.note: bone-in, or cut into smaller pieces

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Fry the ginger until fragrant, then add the garlic and onion and cook until soft.
Add the chicken and cook, stirring, until the outside turns opaque, about 5 minutes.
Add the fish sauce, then both kinds of rice, and stir for 2 minutes.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat and simmer, stirring often so the bottom does not catch, until the chicken is tender and the rice is thick and creamy.
Stir in the kasubha and season with pepper and more fish sauce. Add hot water if it gets too thick.
Serve topped with toasted garlic, egg and scallions, with calamansi to squeeze over.

tips: If you prefer no bones in the bowl, lift the chicken out when tender, shred it and stir it back in.

title: Goto
intro: Rice porridge cooked with tender strips of beef tripe, ginger and garlic, finished with toasted garlic, scallions and egg. It is rich and savory, often eaten with a splash of calamansi and a side of tokwa't baboy.

steps.text: Scrub the tripe all over with the salt and rinse well under running water.
Boil the tripe with the sliced ginger in the 10 cups of water until tender, then drain.
When cool enough to handle, cut the tripe into thin, bite-size strips.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot. Fry the ginger strips, garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the tripe and fish sauce and stir for 2 minutes. Add both kinds of rice and stir to coat.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil, then simmer, stirring often, until thick and creamy.
Stir in the kasubha and taste for salt. Serve topped with toasted garlic, scallions and egg, with calamansi on the side.

tips: A pressure cooker softens the tripe in about 30 minutes. Many cooks boil it a day ahead and keep it in the fridge.

title: Pospas
intro: Visayan chicken rice soup: rice simmered in a ginger chicken broth with shredded chicken, kept loose and brothy rather than thick. It is light and savory, finished with toasted garlic, scallions and egg.

steps.text: Put the chicken, water, ginger and onion in a pot and bring to a boil. Skim, then simmer until the chicken is cooked through.
Lift out the chicken, shred the meat and discard the skin and bones. Strain the broth back into the pot.
Fry the garlic in the oil over medium-low heat until golden and drain on paper towels.
Bring the broth back to a boil, add the rice and simmer, stirring now and then, until the grains are soft and opened but the soup is still brothy.
Return the chicken to the pot and season with the fish sauce and pepper.
Serve topped with toasted garlic, scallions and egg, with calamansi on the side.

tips: If it thickens too much on standing, add hot water; pospas should stay soupy.

title: Goto Batangas
intro: A Batangas-style goto with no rice in the pot: beef tripe and beef simmered into a deep, gingery broth. It is served with plain rice on the side and a sharp dip of soy sauce, calamansi, onion and chili.

steps.text: Scrub the tripe with the salt and rinse well.
Put the tripe, brisket, water, sliced ginger, quartered onion and peppercorns in a large pot. Bring to a boil and skim.
Cover and simmer until both the tripe and beef are tender.
Lift out the meats and cut into bite-size pieces. Strain and keep the broth.
Heat the oil in the pot. Fry the garlic until light golden, then add the ginger strips and chopped onion and cook until soft.
Add the meats and fish sauce and stir for 3 minutes. Pour in the broth and simmer.
Mix the dip ingredients in a small bowl.
Taste the soup for salt and serve topped with scallions, with rice and the dip on the side.

tips: Beef intestines, lung or heart can go in with the tripe if you can get them cleaned; boil them separately first.

title: Pancit molo
intro: Pork and shrimp dumplings in a clear chicken broth with shredded chicken, toasted garlic and scallions. The loose wrapper tails turn silky in the soup, and the garlic gives every spoonful a toasty finish.

steps.text: Simmer the chicken with the water and quartered onion until cooked. Lift out the chicken, shred it and strain the broth.
Meanwhile, mix all the dumpling ingredients except the wrappers until sticky.
Put 1 teaspoon of filling in the center of each wrapper, wet the edges, fold into a triangle and press to seal, leaving the edges loose and frilly.
Heat the oil in a pot and fry the garlic until golden. Scoop out half for topping.
Pour the broth into the pot, add the shredded chicken and fish sauce and bring to a boil.
Drop in the dumplings one at a time and simmer until the filling is cooked and the wrappers turn translucent.
Season with pepper and serve topped with the reserved garlic and scallions.

tips: Freeze extra dumplings on a tray, then bag them; cook straight from frozen for a few minutes longer.

title: Wonton soup
intro: Plump pork and shrimp wontons in a gingery broth with tender bok choy and a drop of sesame oil. It is the clean, simple wonton soup of Chinese-Filipino panciterias.

steps.text: Mix the wonton filling ingredients until sticky.
Put a heaped teaspoon of filling on each wrapper, wet the edges, fold into a triangle and bring the two side corners together, pressing to seal.
Simmer the broth with the ginger so it picks up the flavor. Season with the soy sauce and salt.
Meanwhile, cook the wontons in a separate pot of boiling water until they float, then 2 minutes more.
Add the bok choy to the broth and cook until just tender.
Lift the wontons into bowls, ladle the broth and bok choy over, and finish with scallions and a few drops of sesame oil.

tips: Cooking the wontons in plain water keeps the starch from the wrappers out of the broth, so it stays clear.

title: Almondigas
intro: Pork meatballs simmered in a garlicky broth with soft patola and fine misua noodles. It is a mild, homey soup that kids love, best eaten right away while the noodles are tender.

steps.text: Mix the meatball ingredients and roll into balls about 2 cm across. You should get around 20.
Heat the oil in a pot and fry the garlic and onion until fragrant and soft.
Add the water and bring to a boil.
Drop in the meatballs and simmer until they float and are cooked through.
Add the patola and simmer until tender.
Add the misua, stir gently and cook just until soft. Season with the fish sauce.
Top with scallions and serve right away.

tips: Misua keeps drinking up the broth, so cook it at the last minute and have hot water ready when reheating.

title: Misua at patola
intro: A light everyday soup of soft patola and fine misua noodles with ribbons of egg. It is quick, gentle and a little sweet from the gourd.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot and cook the garlic, onion and tomato until the tomato softens.
Add the water and bring to a boil.
Add the patola and simmer until tender.
Season with the salt, add the misua and cook until soft.
Pour the beaten eggs in a thin stream while gently stirring so they set into ribbons.
Season with pepper, top with scallions and serve right away.

tips: Choose patola that feels heavy and firm; old ones turn spongy and bitter.

title: Suam na tulya
intro: Tiny freshwater clams cooked in rice washing with a lot of ginger, finished with chili leaves or malunggay. The broth is cloudy, sweet from the clams and sharp with ginger.

steps.text: Rinse the purged clams several times in fresh water and drain.
Heat the oil in a pot and fry the ginger until fragrant, then add the garlic and onion and cook until soft.
Pour in the rice washing and bring to a boil.
Add the clams, cover and boil until the shells open.
Discard any that stay shut. Taste the broth, then season with fish sauce and pepper.
Turn off the heat, stir in the leaves and serve with rice.

tips: Soak the clams in salted water for an hour so they spit out their sand, and lift them out of the water instead of pouring them into a colander.

title: Chicken sotanghon soup
intro: Glass noodles and shredded chicken in a golden broth colored with annatto, with carrots, cabbage and mushrooms. It is light and slurpable, topped with toasted garlic and scallions.

steps.text: Simmer the chicken in the water until cooked. Lift out, shred the meat and strain the broth.
Meanwhile, soak the sotanghon in water until soft, then drain and cut into shorter lengths with scissors.
Warm the oil and annatto seeds in a pot over low heat until the oil turns deep orange. Discard the seeds.
Fry the garlic and onion in the annatto oil until fragrant. Add the mushrooms and carrot and cook for 2 minutes.
Pour in the broth, add the chicken and fish sauce and bring to a boil.
Add the sotanghon and cabbage and simmer until the noodles turn clear.
Season with pepper and serve topped with scallions.

tips: Sotanghon soaks up broth fast; if making ahead, keep the noodles separate and add them when reheating.

title: La Paz batchoy
intro: Fresh egg noodles in a rich pork broth seasoned with shrimp paste, topped with sliced pork, liver, crushed chicharon, toasted garlic and scallions. It is deeply savory, a little sweet and very filling.

steps.text: Cover the bones with water, boil for 5 minutes, then drain and rinse.
Return the bones to the pot with the 12 cups of water, the pork shoulder and onion. Bring to a boil, skim, then simmer until the shoulder is tender.
Lift out the shoulder and let it cool, then slice thinly.
Add the liver to the simmering broth and cook through. Lift out and slice thinly.
Strain the broth back into the pot. Stir in the shrimp paste, fish sauce, sugar and pepper and keep it at a simmer.
Blanch the noodles in boiling water in portions for about 1 minute, then drain into bowls.
Top the noodles with pork and liver. Crack in a raw egg if using, then ladle over the boiling broth so it cooks the egg.
Finish with chicharon, toasted garlic and scallions and serve at once.

tips: Add the chicharon just before eating so it stays crunchy. Leftover broth freezes well for the next batch.

title: Batchoy Tagalog
intro: Sliced pork and liver in a ginger broth with misua and chili leaves. It is quick, peppery and savory, a different dish from the noodle batchoy of the Visayas.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot and fry the ginger, garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the pork and cook until lightly browned, about 5 minutes. Add the fish sauce and stir.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil and skim, then simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the liver and cook just until no longer pink inside.
Add the misua and cook until soft.
Turn off the heat, stir in the leaves and season with pepper. Serve hot.

tips: Overcooked liver turns grainy; add it near the end and take the pot off the heat as soon as it is done.

title: Chicken mami
intro: Egg noodles in a clear ginger chicken broth, topped with shredded chicken, bok choy, a boiled egg and toasted garlic. It is the classic merienda noodle soup, light but satisfying.

steps.text: Put the chicken, water, onion, ginger and peppercorns in a pot. Bring to a boil, skim, then simmer until the chicken is tender.
Lift out the chicken, shred the meat and discard the bones. Strain the broth back into the pot and season with the fish sauce.
Blanch the bok choy in the simmering broth and lift it out.
Cook the noodles in a separate pot of boiling water according to the package, then drain.
Divide the noodles among bowls. Top with chicken, bok choy and egg, ladle over the hot broth and finish with scallions and toasted garlic.

tips: Rinse fresh noodles briefly in hot water before cooking to wash off the excess flour, so the broth stays clear.

title: Beef mami
intro: Egg noodles in a beefy broth scented with star anise and ginger, topped with slices of slow-simmered brisket and bok choy. Rich, gently sweet and fragrant.

steps.text: Cover the brisket with water, boil for 5 minutes, then drain and rinse.
Return the beef to the pot with the 10 cups of water, onion, ginger and star anise. Bring to a boil and skim.
Cover and simmer until the brisket is tender.
Lift out the beef, let it rest for a few minutes and slice it across the grain.
Strain the broth, return it to the pot and season with the soy sauce, sugar and fish sauce. Blanch the bok choy in it.
Cook the noodles in a separate pot of boiling water, then drain into bowls.
Top with beef and bok choy, ladle over the hot broth and finish with scallions and garlic.

tips: Chill the broth overnight and lift off the fat for a cleaner soup; the beef also slices more neatly when cold.

title: Asado mami
intro: Egg noodles in a clear chicken broth topped with sweet-savory braised pork asado and bok choy. A spoonful of the asado sauce over the noodles makes each bowl glossy and rich.

steps.text: Put the pork, soy sauce, sugar, hoisin, garlic, star anise and water in a small pot. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer, turning the pork now and then.
Uncover and simmer until the sauce is thick and glossy and coats the pork.
Let the pork rest, then slice thinly. Keep the sauce.
Meanwhile, simmer the broth with the ginger and onion. Season with the fish sauce and strain.
Blanch the bok choy in the broth. Cook the noodles in a separate pot of boiling water and drain.
Divide the noodles among bowls, add the broth, then top with asado slices, bok choy, a spoonful of the sauce, scallions and garlic.

tips: The asado keeps for 4 days in the fridge and is also good on rice or in siopao.
